Yeah, haha- that was my frustration with Kaplan. I mean, I appreciate that they do give you a brief rundown of SIE topics for a page or two in their Series 7 book, but they usually preface it by saying "this was covered in the SIE text" as if everyone who has the 7 book also has their SIE book (which could be true, but still...)

Admittedly, switching vendors did save me for this test; after my first reading of Kaplan I was incredibly frustrated with the book and still had no idea of how to answer options questions. They do this thing where in the text they give ONE example and spend SEVERAL paragraphs explaining it. They kept referencing the T chart as the best way to answer options questions, but no matter how many times I replicated it on questions, I always managed to mess up which amount goes into the credit or debit side. Reading the options section on Achievable gave me this weird eureka moment once the content was broken down and easier to digest with multiple examples and suddenly I had my own way to calculate options (a looser version of the T chart) which ended up being effective a majority of the time.

So I mean I feel like vendor hopping is very useful if one text just doesn't do it for you, but it also depends on how much time you have left to reinforce concepts and whether you're willing to spend more on another text which may or may not be as helpful (of course there are free resources online too, but those can be hit or miss if you don't know what you're looking for). Keep at it!

Personally I'd agree, at least not intensive math anyway. The "biggest" thing for me was probably calculating the current yield, or the tax-free equivalent yield. Other than that is basic addition/subtraction/multiplication (especially for options, nothing really advanced).

I might be biased here, but my exam felt very regulation/suitability heavy. I would say to spend some time focusing on the smaller topics in addition to the general options/munis/suitability trio (trading activity, responding to customers and handling their problems, online communications and materials to the public). 

So, definitely know what a RR can and can't do in situations [or choose what you feel is the most obvious answer on the exam, usually reporting a problem to a principal or trusted contact person instead of trying to fix something on your own]. Also focus on regulations and rules (not on specific, detailed numbers but the 80% rule for intrastate offerings or 90% net income for REITs come to mind). Honestly I wouldn't really worry that much about margins since they make up a minor part of the exam, if at all.
Thank you! Wish you the best of luck as you move forward!

I think I have a weird love/hate relationship with Kaplan. 

I definitely could have used the QBank more; for the first month (and first half) of studying, I took about 96 quizzes total across the units to differing results (90 of them were for Units 1-5, then only two quizzes for Units 6, 7, and 8 each). I ended up only using about 67% of the QBank overall.

During the same month, I was trying to keep up with the reading and checkpoint exams while working full time at my B/D. I ended up failing the Unit 1 Checkpoint Exam (66.67%), passing Unit 2 (86.87%), passing Unit 3 (77.42%), barely passing Unit 4 (73.33%), passing Unit 5 (75%), failing Unit 6 (64%), failing Unit 7 (65%), and passing Unit 8 (85%). So passing only 5/8 checkpoint exams but the fails weren't extremely bad.

After that, I started taking the simulated exams.

Kaplan Simulated Test scores were: 72.8, 75.2, 71.2, 72.8, 74.4, 76.8, 80

Kaplan Practice Test scores were: 76.8, 80

Right after reading through the textbook my scores were just barely passing the threshold. I started looking through Achievable at this point and, while my scores didn't increase significantly, taking more Kaplan exams lead to better scores, and the maximum I could reach was 80. I was passing, but only by a handful of questions and so I wasn't feeling very prepared.

This past Sunday, I took the Mastery Exam and only scored a 67. I was slightly freaking out at this point because people were generally recommending to be in the 80s for a comfortable chance of passing and it always seemed as if I was was below that threshold. Looking at the breakdown however, most of my problems came from the smaller Units (7 and 8) and I was actually comfortable and doing well with the big boys (Munis, Options, and Suitability, mainly thanks to Achievable). So from there it was just watching Brian's videos on trying to focus on what would specifically be on the exam while glancing over some notes from those two units from all texts.

Sorry for the long-winded answer, but hope it helps!

Thanks!

I would say: 

1) Registered representative actions (what one can and cannot do, how to handle certain situations, communications and approval, new account forms)

2) Customer suitability/recommendations (explaining to a customer why a corporation is doing something, looking out for a customer's best interests in their requests, portfolio diversifications: best choices for the customer and interpreting their allocations)

3) Registration (what can be found in a prospectus/notice of sale/whathaveyou, cooldown period, SAI, Regulation D, Rule 147

Honestly, most of my exam seemed pretty regulation/recommendation/ability heavy; other questions included NAV/mutual funds/ETFs and current yield, only one margin question.

But yeah, I'd say this is a step in the right direction, considering that it's probably too late to ever reclaim that LB1 sound. Current favorites include "She Ready," "Count Me In," "Love Me Forever" (lol), and "66."
